metadata.title: An Agent That Finishes First Can Be Worse Than One That Stops.
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: does an agent's confident 'done' mean it checked everything? Lands the carry-out that a completion report only tallies what succeeded, not what existed — ask for the count, not just the completion.
metadata.anchor_pair: B03 -> B09 (the six-bullet brief with three unopened dissenting documents: planted as the case that breaks the wrong guess; returned via an inventory check that turns the skip into a counted, stamped mismatch)
metadata.one_flag: B07 - the report-only-tallies-successes structure assumes the tool doesn't separately log skips; some do, and you can't tell which from a confident 'done' alone

beats.narration_text: Someone assumes a confident 'done' means the scan was complete. It might not be — the scan can be partial and still get reported as done. So what happens to the part it missed?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'A confident done from Claude means the scan was complete, right?', hesitates on 'complete', corrects to 'partial'

props.text:
A confident done
from Claude means
the scan was
complete, right?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('complete' -> 'partial') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: An agent can read ninety files, finish the job, and report 'done' — in exactly the same confident tone whether it saw everything in scope or missed a third of it.

shot.new_visual_element: the same 'DONE' stamp over two different coverage counts, 90/90 and 60/90

production_viz.label: Same confident stamp, different coverage
production_viz.mechanic: Two panels side by side, each a file-count readout: '90 / 90' on the left, '60 / 90' on the right. An identical DONE stamp drops onto both at the same moment. Caption beneath: 'same confident tone either way'.

beats.narration_text: So the natural read: if the agent says the task is complete, it must have gone through everything there was to go through. A confident finish feels like proof of a full pass.

shot.new_visual_element: a checklist, a checkmark forming under 'task complete'

production_viz.label: The natural guess
production_viz.mechanic: A short checklist block with the heading TASK COMPLETE. A confident checkmark forms beneath it. Caption: 'complete = everything covered?'.

beats.narration_text: Here's the case that breaks it. An agent drafted a six-bullet brief with a clear recommendation, and it shipped to leadership. Two days later, someone found three dissenting documents sitting in a subfolder the agent never opened — one of them said the opposite of the recommendation. No error had ever appeared.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR - a folder tree, five documents glowing teal 'read', three documents in a dissenting subfolder glowing crimson 'unopened', a summary box glowing COMPLETE

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR - the folder tree
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. A simple folder tree: a top node PROJECT with five document leaves glowing TEAL (read); a subfolder node DISSENTING holding three leaves glowing CRIMSON (never opened). A SUMMARY box at the bottom glows teal COMPLETE. THIS EXACT COMPOSITION RETURNS AT B09, restamped.

beats.narration_text: Here's the mechanism. An agent works through a job one operation at a time: open a file, success. Summarize it, success. Move to the next, success. Each step only reports on itself.

shot.new_visual_element: a chain of operation boxes - READ, SUMMARIZE, NEXT - filling teal with a checkmark in sequence

production_viz.label: The per-operation success chain
production_viz.mechanic: A horizontal chain of three boxes labeled READ, SUMMARIZE, NEXT. Each fills TEAL with a small checkmark as it completes in sequence; the chain repeats once for a second file.

beats.narration_text: But the agent doesn't know what it couldn't reach. A subfolder it lacked permission for. A scanned page that wouldn't parse as text. A file that scrolled past when a long listing got cut off.

shot.new_visual_element: the teal operation chain on the left, three crimson file icons on the right - no access, unreadable scan, not listed

production_viz.label: The boundary of what was reached
production_viz.mechanic: The TEAL operation chain from B04 sits on the left. On the right, three file icons in CRIMSON: NO ACCESS, UNREADABLE SCAN, NOT LISTED. A dashed vertical line separates what the agent saw from what it didn't.

beats.narration_text: A crash tells you something went wrong — you see the failure. A silent omission doesn't. The agent that stops and flags a file it couldn't read is giving you information. The one that quietly skips it and reports 'done' is giving you none.

shot.new_visual_element: two columns - CRASH, a visible error box, vs SILENT OMISSION, a green complete box with an arrow to gap in brief

production_viz.label: Crash vs. silent omission
production_viz.mechanic: Two columns side by side: left CRASH shows a CRIMSON error box — the problem is visible. Right SILENT OMISSION shows a TEAL COMPLETE box; an arrow beneath it points to GAP IN BRIEF, labeled in CRIMSON.

beats.narration_text: One flag: this is about agents whose completion report only tallies successful operations. Some tools do log every skipped or unreadable file in a separate section — but you can't tell which kind you're looking at from a confident 'done' alone. You have to check whether skips get surfaced at all.

shot.new_visual_element: THE FLAG - a single terracotta flag marker over two paths, one where a skip lands in a visible log, one where it disappears

production_viz.label: THE ONE FLAG - does the skip get logged?
production_viz.mechanic: A single terracotta FLAG marker over the beat, the reel's only hedge, labeled as one. Two branching paths from one file icon: one path ends in a visible SKIPPED LOG entry; the other ends in nothing, the icon simply fading out. Caption: 'you can't tell which from done alone'.

beats.narration_text: Maya ran an agent over twelve client PDFs to draft a digest. It read nine — three were scanned images it couldn't parse — and reported the digest done. Those three held the revised targets. The digest shipped with the old numbers, and nothing in the report said anything was missing.

shot.new_visual_element: twelve file icons, nine teal read, three crimson scan-unreadable, an arrow to a DIGEST document labeled old targets

production_viz.label: Maya: 12 PDFs, 9 read, 3 skipped
production_viz.mechanic: Twelve file icons in a grid: nine fill TEAL with a small check, three stay CRIMSON labeled SCAN — UNREADABLE. An arrow from the nine leads to a DIGEST document reading OLD TARGETS. A label Q4 REVISION points to one of the three CRIMSON files.

beats.narration_text: Go back to the six-bullet brief: ask for the inventory instead of the summary — documents in scope, documents opened, documents skipped. Three skipped against twenty-six in scope is the mismatch that catches it. But a matching inventory doesn't prove every document was read correctly, only that none went silently missing — and one skipped file doesn't mean the whole brief is wrong, just that one document needs a second pass.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS - the same folder tree, the three dissenting documents now stamped CONFIRMED SKIPPED, two dimmed captions beneath

production_viz.label: The inventory, then both directions
production_viz.mechanic: THE B03 ANCHOR RETURNS: the same folder tree, the three DISSENTING leaves now each carrying a small log stamp CONFIRMED: SKIPPED. Beneath, two dimmed captions fade in: 'MATCHING COUNT != EVERY DOC READ RIGHT' and 'ONE SKIP != WHOLE BRIEF WRONG'.

beats.narration_text: A confident 'done' only tells you what finished — never what got skipped. Ask for the count, not just the completion.

props.quote: A confident 'done' only tells you what finished — never what got skipped. Ask for the count, not just the completion.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. I'm using an agent to process a folder of files and summarize them. Give me the exact three questions to ask afterward — about scope, what was processed, and what was skipped — so I can catch anything it silently missed, and tell me what a mismatch should make me do next. Liam, in for Bear.
